correctness.rationale: Ren–Chen Theorem 1.2 reduces exactly-two-distinct-prime near-perfect integers to the three listed families plus 40. For odd U, U>2g>c leaves only U=q or q². The square-repunit solutions (g,ℓ,root)=(7,4,20),(3,5,11) cannot supply a Mersenne prime; U=q leaves a digit larger than the permitted range in all three families. For odd g and ℓ=2m with odd m>1, U_m(g) and (g^m+1)/(g+1) are nontrivial coprime odd factors. For 4|ℓ, (g+1)Q divides U with Q=(g²+1)/2 odd, coprime to g+1 and >g; this forces g+1=2^s. The valuation gives odd part of U >2g^(ℓ−1)/((g+1)ℓ), greater than Q² for ℓ≥8 by checking ℓ=8 and monotonicity. This contradicts the odd exponent bound. At ℓ=4, the q² case conflicts with the required Type-A valuation; Q=q exceeds the digit and excludes Type A, and Type B gives q≤g<Q (the strict q<g written at this step can be weakened to ≤ without affecting the contradiction). For Type C the only possible valuations a are 2s−2,2s−1; the resulting difference 2^s−2 or 2^(2s−1)+2^s−2 cannot be the required power of two, with s=2 excluded from the first case by a≥s+1. Independent finite check of divisors U of 40 found only (g,ℓ,U)=(3,4,40); sigma(40)=90, so d=10. The frozen parameter scan is regression evidence only and was inspected, not run.
residual_risks: Relies on the two cited theorems; the Ljunggren statement was checked through the modern full-text citation, not the original printing. No claims for two digits or larger prime support.

evidence: Ren–Chen classify all eligible N as families plus 40 without a repdigit condition. The even-base record gives exactly-two-digit necessity whenever there are at least two digits. The Ω-bounded record includes 40 but does not classify its repdigit family for unbounded Ω.
broader_coverage.reasoning: The even-base subgroup is covered by stronger prior work. The all-N classification only gives families to analyze, and a bound on multiplicity Ω is not a bound on the claimed scope ω=2.

evidence: The bounded odd-base proof needs c≤8 and g+1≤10, then enumerates 31 candidate N. Ljunggren rules out one odd-square-repunit case; it imposes no such restriction for the even repunits.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: Combining the bounded and even-base results still leaves every odd base g≥11. Resolving these requires the new uniform parity, coprimality and valuation argument, not just taking a corollary of the cited classifications.

originality.rationale: The tuple 40=(1111)_3 and the even-base exclusion both have exact prior coverage. The distinct claim is exclusion of every unbounded odd base, including odd bases above 9; the strongest bounded odd-base result does not imply that exclusion, and the general two-prime near-perfect classification does not impose the representation condition. The prior odd-base record should be credited explicitly in any account of the extension.
residual_risks: The original Ljunggren printing was not inspected directly. An equivalent unbounded odd-base result in other or unindexed work remains possible. Directory dates do not in themselves establish priority.

value.rationale: The results for bounded odd bases and for all even bases leave a natural unbounded family open. Resolving it gives a complete representation classification within two-prime near-perfect numbers and explains why the known base-3 exception cannot recur at large odd bases. The contribution is that uniform exclusion, not rediscovery of 40.
residual_risks: No claim about greater prime support or all short representations.
